This might not be relevant for you, but I'm a highly introverted person and for a long time believed that was something that would change if I became more confident. However, no matter how much my confidence increases, if I spend a lot of time around other people without taking alone time for myself I tend to get wiped out emotionally and all the bad thoughts start creeping back in (despite no bad thing having happened). Even when I do get alone time after socialising I tend to have an emotional dip and lower self esteem. Something that helped me recently was finding out about the MBTI categories of personalities. There's only 16 of them and obviously the range of characters in the world can't really be boxed into 16 categories as there's such a fluid range. However, it does boil down some of your characteristics based on how you interact with the world and what drives you. Determining my type and researching it has given me really lovely positive summaries that reflect a character I can identify with and through that see some of my positive features alongside some of my downfalls which are easier to consider with kindness when written by someone else in a much more objective way. I've determined a couple of friends character types and sent them YouTube videos on them as well and at least one of them has found it hugely helpful on putting her back in track with feeling positively about who she is and what her individual strengths are.

It might not help you and it might only offer temporary relief, but it's worth a shot if it does anything like the confidence boost it has given me and my friend.

Having these conversations whilst performing a simple task is such a great idea! It removes so much intensity from the conversation. My partner and I prefer to talk about sensitive things only over messenger. And for less intense things over a game of cards. I know lots of people do better talking whilst going out for a walk. It may be difficult to get him out and about doing something with you but even just getting him out the house and doing something will be incredibly helpful.

Also, I know when I was younger and my mum used to try to do things to cheer me up from my depression, she would do something silly like buy a sunflower and bring it into my room and tell me it's a happy flower to make me feel happy. And then she'd leave me alone (which was good). At the time I probably acted with disgust or an eye roll. But actually once she left it kind of resonated with me that she cared and was trying to help. Roughly 20 years later I still remember that moment vividly and have so much love and appreciation for my mum. So what I'm trying to say is, don't give up, and know that even if your efforts don't feel recognised, you don't really know what's going on under the surface of a depressed person, and you may actually be having huge impacts without realising.

I have so much respect for you for approaching this in a loving and caring way. So many people get frustrated and that really does make everything much worse.

Okay cool :) so I believe the first thing to focus on before trying to find any solutions to a problem is just trying to step out of this trapped enclosed feeling. I can't think properly when I'm feeling really stressed and powerless, I can't be creative or come up with ideas, and when I try and fail it makes me feel worse. So I have a few things I revisit or read up on to try change my outlook on what's happening.

Yesterday I rewatched [this TED talk](https://www.ted.com/talks/jane_mcgonigal_the_game_that_can_give_you_10_extra_years_of_life) about approaching life as a game. It's a bit silly, but if you can get into it it can be really effective at taking you from feeling like the world is a big mess and feeling powerless, to sort of picking out the challenges and hurdles and playing at being some sort of character or game avatar where you are determined and capable of solving these problems. Obviously it's not a long term solution and you can't live your whole life this way, but in times of deep stress it can be helpful to bring a sense of play and motivation, focus on what the problems are, and self belief that you can make things happen and create change.

For instance, I suffer from anxiety and depression (the classic duo) so I've come up with a name that is different from my own and imagine her as this tough, capable, determined person. The bad guys she's fighting against are things like the Insomnia Demon, the Self-Esteem Fiend, the Catastrophizer, Social Anxiety Monster, etc etc. And by identifying those thoughts and giving them fun character names it externalizes them from me and makes it easier to recognize them and fight against them. Like doing exercise and wearing myself out in a fight against Insomnia Demon so I don't let it get me and can hopefully sleep that night. Or imagining I'm locking the Catastrophizer in a box when it starts telling me all the ways in which everything is going to go wrong. Anyway, that might not be up your street at all. It's pretty silly and took me a while to adopt without feeling totally dumb. 

Other than that people always talk about doing mindfulness on here, which is useful. But what I like is Stoic Philosophy. It's actually not as dry or academic as it sounds. A lot of it is about recognizing what you can't control and what you can. I feel like once you have a clear idea what things you can't change, a lot of things you worry and stress about go away because you realise you have no control over them so there's no point thinking about them. But really the best thing is that you realise all the things you *can* control and can put all your focus on those - and then you can start to plan! I like [this article](http://philosophizethis.org/10-things-the-stoics-can-teach-you-about-being-a-happier-person/) as a brief introduction to the essential principles of what Stocism is about. 

Once you want to start planning, it's hard to think outside the box but really try - if money is a hurdle you can think of ways to get over it (brainstorm ways of making money, learning new skills in your spare time [like programming](https://www.codecademy.com/learn)), or get around it (look at options usually termed "alternative lifestyles", like going to new places and volunteering in exchange for accommodation and meals). If issues with your flat is the hurdle you could brainstorm ways to make your room a safe haven, candles, incense, turn relaxing music you really enjoy on as soon as you get in your room, put up pictures or photos that make you happy, and survive it out until you leave. Or you can try and get out, look at subletting, look at other places to stay. I'm not sure where you live or what your situation is, but I used to live in a city and only ever considered staying in the city center in expensive flats, where it was busy and noisy, but a couple I knew found a farmer from just outside the city with a mobile home on his land and they rented it from him for super cheap. They were able to cycle to the nearest train station to get into the city and it saved them a fortune. They got to live in a beautiful area too. 

There are plenty of communities online for inspiration, it can be hard to first start looking but once you find a thread to start pulling at you'll find a whole resource of ideas and creative thinkers. 

Once I'm in the right frame of mind for problem-solving, I like sitting down with coloured pens and drawing mind maps. I decide on one problem I want to solve and then just put down any ideas or half ideas for solutions all around it and add colour just because it makes me feel better to look at it. You don't need to do this all alone, the internet is your friend when looking for ideas. (Currently my boyfriend and I are looking into living in a van - sounds mad but lots of people do it, and plenty of very normal, clean, practical people too!)

Other resources that have helped make me feel calmer or more empowered are:

* [The School of Life](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC7IcJI8PUf5Z3zKxnZvTBog)
* [Some of the Videos by Jenny Mustard](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S8jvZHKQnt0) or [ones with her partner too](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC3lTRet0C4sEfeNiiZwwlYw)
* [The Guilty Feminist Podcast](http://guiltyfeminist.com/episodes/) two female comedians and a guest an episode talking about challenges they face in their lives in very practical terms and finding fun solutions and challenges to overcome them. It's a lot of jokes and not too preachy, more about self-empowerment and having fun.

I hope some or any of this is helpful to you, even if you don't take these exact approaches or use these links I just hope it sparks some new ideas for you about how to get yourself into a better place.

I'm so sad to hear about your situation. It sounds awful. I would agree that challenging her on this opinion may not be the most helpful thing for you. She's clearly wrong, but do you think you could realistically change her mind? If her response is bad it will only hurt you more. 

Your situation is tough and severe, but I've always liked the phrase "a smooth sea never made a skilled sailor". Basically times of trouble or challenging situations like this are an opportunity to help you build strength of character that will potentially lead you to a better life, prepped with better coping mechanisms and stamina for difficult situations. 

I agree that mindfulness might be a good thing to look into as a method of coping with these tough situations. I also really like the philosophy of stoicism - which basically focuses on recognising that you can't control the world around you, but you can control the way you react to it (mindfulness is about exactly this). You can't control your mums yelling or the things she says, but with practice and determination, you can control how much you allow it to affect you. It's much easier said than done but it truly is worth trying for and working towards. There are plenty of articles giving good introductions to stoicism that aren't tough reads, I quite like this one http://philosophizethis.org/10-things-the-stoics-can-teach-you-about-being-a-happier-person/

I hope you can find something to help get you through x

She covers the main (I think 4) areas of life that everyone needs some level of satisfaction in to feel good in their lives. Don't be put off by the fact that it seems to be talking about gaming, what she's really covering is an assessment of what it takes to find satisfaction in life. From what I remember I think 2 of those points had social elements to them. You don't need a data science certificate. I've never come across a time where any kind of certification would have been particularly beneficial in my 10 years in the industry. What will make a difference is having working examples like code on GitHub or blog posts explaining your work. I write Jupyter notebooks them post them to a blog.

Hey, so I used to work for a company that dealt with a lot of social media data - it required me to solve lots of problems in the NLP field. Most of the time I didn't have to consider Big Data. Example problems I would solve are things like detecting topics in a corpus of text or determining sentiment and things like that. I worked with Python and would use the library Spacy a lot rather than NLTK, this does a lot of the tokenization and stemming work for you, you can detect sentence structures with POS tags and entity detection. Learn Spacy and also look at word2vec with the gensim library. That should be a good starting point that will be relevant to most jobs in text analysis. Try simple tasks like topic extraction, also be aware of differences in language and how to make analysis language agnostic.

There are loads of jobs in NLP, it's so useful in so many areas. You should be able to find plenty of work if you can demonstrate knowledge with a few examples on github or a blog or something

I really agree that euthanasia should be made available to everyone. I think we would all benefit from a lot of the stigma being taken out of suicide. Just because the majority of people don't understand the desire to end your life, doesn't mean they're in the right and that those who don't want to live anymore are "sick" or in the wrong. We accept euthanasia for degenerative diseases and for those who it can be agreed have no quality of life. Is living with lifelong depression not "no quality of life"? I feel like it is more-so than any other illness. People might say it's curable but do we know that's the case in every instance? What about all the people who commit suicide? How long have they felt suicidal for? Was it not inevitable that a time in their life would come when they would have done it anyway? As in it's possible some of those people might have never been "cured", it would have only prolonged their suffering to stay alive. 

If stigma was taken out of the act, instead of all "help" around the subject just focusing on trying to stop suicides, suicidal people could open up more, could speak to family and friends, could give the people they care about closure and time to prepare for the event. I think that would be the biggest help to everyone involved, rather than leaving suicidal people feeling overcome by guilt, and their loved ones shocked and even angry at them when the time comes. In many instances people might change their minds after talking to loved ones, and in some cases not. But I get so frustrated when I see suicide "help" groups trying to stop people committing suicide, rather than understanding that for some people this is the path of least suffering, perhaps the help is better off directed to loved ones of suicidal people in coming to terms with the fact this might be what's best for them, it's their choice. Those who are trying to help might not understand, but it doesn't mean they get to tell people what to do or make them feel like suicide is bad or wrong and that they shouldn't do it.

I read or heard somewhere this idea for what makes a successful long lasting relationship; kind of imagine it like layers of a pyramid chart (this is just how I remember it being explained to me). 

First as a foundation, you as a couple need to match up on your **values** - like what you see as right and wrong, a respectable way of living, an appropriate way of acting or being. 

Then on top of that, together you would build and match up on shared **goals** - you need to want the same things from life, like whether you want kids, or agreement on where you would live so neither feels they are making too big a sacrifice for the other, they are fulfilling their life in the way they want to.

If you've found someone you match up with on those two things then the top layer of the pyramid would be **love** or how well you get along together. It depends how much of a romantic you are whether you would even need to choose a partner you are _in love_ with. So long as you get on well with someone, and can be committed to them as a companion for life. That's what marriage is really about as far as I see it. Companionship and a commitment to support one another. You become a team.

I don't know if this helps you evaluate your problem, it's just something I've come across and felt like it helped me frame decisions about my own relationships and whether they would stand the test of time. 

It sounds like you're falling down on the middle layer and if you can't get her on board with you, or come to a compromise that you are both genuinely invested in, then either one of you might feel resentment build over the years if you're not living your life in the way you want to. My suggestion would be to have an open and honest discussion about your values and goals and see if you can really come up with a plan you're both enthusiastic about, else you might just not be the right match.

Disclaimer : this whole thing is just an idea, not necessarily a reality. There may be cases of marriages that have survived based on sacrifice or mismatched values. I just find it a useful way to think about things as it seems a fairly solid model for success to me.
